content.title: Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II operators
content.text: From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Operates F-35A, F-35B and F-35C variants (United States) Operates F-35A and F-35B variants (Italy, Japan) Operates F-35A variant only (Australia, Denmark, Netherlands, Norway, South Korea) Operates F-35B variant only (United Kingdom) Operates F-35I variant only (Israel) Awaiting delivery (F-35A: Belgium, Canada, Czech Republic, Finland, Germany, Greece, Poland, Romania, Switzerland; F-35A & F-35B: Singapore) The Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II is a family of stealth multirole fighters that first entered service with the United States in 2015. The aircraft has been ordered by program partner nations, including the United Kingdom, Italy, Norway, and Australia, and also through the Department of Defense's Foreign Military Sales program, including Japan, South Korea, and Israel. The units that operate or plan on operating the aircraft are listed below. One of the RAAF's first two F-35As in December 2014 The F-35I Adir (accompanied by a 253 Squadron F-16I Sufa) on its debut flight in Israel, December 2016 Dutch F-35A in July 2013 F-35 in 41st Training Air Base in Dęblin, Poland during the 2020 acquisition deal signing ceremony Australia Royal Australian Air Force – 72 operational.[1] RAAF Base Williamtown, New South Wales No. 2 OCU[2] No. 3 Squadron[3][4] No. 77 Squadron[5] RAAF Base Tindal, Northern Territory No. 75 Squadron[6] Belgium Belgian Air Force – 4 operational, 34 planned.[7][8] Florennes Air Base 2nd Tactical Wing Kleine Brogel Air Base 10th Tactical Wing Canada Royal Canadian Air Force – 88 ordered in January 2023. First aircraft to arrive in 2026, first squadron operational in 2029 and full fleet operational by 2032 to 2034.[9][10][11] Czech Republic Czech Air Force – The U.S. State Department approved a possible sale to the Czech Republic of F-35 aircraft, munitions and related equipment worth up to $5.62 billion, according to a 29 June 2023 announcement.[12] On 29 January 2024, the Czech government signed a memorandum of understanding with the United States for the purchase of F-35A fighters.[13] Denmark Royal Danish Air Force – 17 delivered out of 43 planned.[14][15][16] The first four aircraft are expected to be flown from Luke Air Force Base, starting in 2021 for the training of Danish pilots. The first four aircraft arrived at Skrydstrup Air Base in September 2023 with 13 more having been delivered to Skrydstrup in January 2025.[17] Full operational capability for the first 27 is expected in 2027; VFA-147[119] Potential operators[edit] Morocco Royal Moroccan Air Force – It is reported that Morocco is interested in purchasing F-35s in a US$18 billion deal to counter Algeria's Su-57 acquisition.[120][121] India Indian Air Force – In February 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump had offered the F-35 to Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India,[122] which as of March 2025, was also mulling a competing offer from Russia's Sukhoi Su-57.[123] However, in late July 2025, Bloomberg reported that India has already rejected its requirement of the aircraft. While the Indian Ministry of Defence has not confirmed any of this, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs maintained that India has not held any formal discussions about the aircraft's procurement with the USA.[124][125] Former potential operators[edit] Republic of China Republic of China Air Force – In 2011, it was reported that Taiwan would procure a 5th Generation fighter such as the F-35.[126] A renewed push for purchasing the F-35 happened in early 2017,[127] and again in March 2018.[128] However, by November 2018 it was reported that the Taiwanese military leadership abandoned the F-35 program in favor of the F-16V Viper. Reportedly, the decision was motivated by concerns about industry independence, and Chinese espionage concerns.[129] Spain Spanish Navy / Spanish Air Force – In 2023, the Spanish government included €6.25 billion in its budget requirements to begin the process of replacing combat aircraft used by both the Navy and the Air Force. The Navy's plan was to retire its AV-8B Harrier aircraft by 2030; due to Juan Carlos I being a STOVL aircraft carrier, the only feasible alternative to the Harrier was the F-35B. The Air Force were also looking at the F-35A to replace its F/A-18 Hornets while the Future Combat Air System was under development. However, in 2025, the government elected to end any interest in the procurement of either version of the F-35. For the Air Force, Spain instead elected to new purchases of the Eurofighter Typhoon, while the Navy faced the potential of a fixed-wing aviation gap after 2030.[130] Thailand Royal Thai Air Force – 8 or 12 planned to replace F-16A/B Block 15 ADF in service. On 12 January 2022, Thailand's cabinet approved a budget for the first four F-35A, estimated at 13.8 billion baht in FY2023.[131][132][133] On 22 May 2023 The United States Department of Defense has implied it will turn down Thailand's bid to buy F-35 fighter jets, and instead offer F-16V Viper and F-15EX Eagle II fighters, a Royal Thai Air Force source said.[134] Turkey Turkish Air Force – 4 F-35A delivered and withheld[135][136] at Luke Air Force Base. 30 F-35s were ordered,[137] of up to 100 total planned.[138][139] Future purchases have been banned by the U.S. with contracts canceled by early 2020.[136] On 1 February 2024 the U.S. expressed a willingness to readmit Turkey into the F-35 program in the event of a satisfactory resolution of the S-400 issue.[140] United Arab Emirates United Arab Emirates Air Force – Up to 50 had been planned, although the sale was suspended and reviewed by the Biden administration.[141][142] In December 2021 UAE withdrew from the purchase of F-35s as it did not agree to the additional contract terms added by the US.[143][144] Ship-based platforms[edit] Ship-based platform activation includes:[145] F-35B F-35C United States Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Carl Vinson USS Theodore Roosevelt USS Abraham Lincoln USS George Washington USS John C. Kennedy (planned for 2028) Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II procurement ^ In June 2025, the UK government announced that, as part of the second tranche of 27 aircraft it planned to procure, it would purchase 15 new F-35Bs, swapping the additional 12 airframes for an identical number of F-35As. Intended to operate as part of 207 Squadron, the Lightning Operational Conversion Unit, the F-35A would primarily be utilised as a training platform, thanks to its increased endurance over the F-35B.
